item.title: Elevator draft, agaiin: Re: Elevator draft, agaiin
item.content:encoded:
It would be good to keep in mind I'm new to the foundation and haven't made an scp yet, so take my criticism with a grain of salt, but these are all the things I noticed while reading it, in the same order as the article.

my (nitpicky) criticism
 my (nitpicky) criticism

I don't get why it would be esoteric? seems like it would be safe, because they can just keep it in one place, no one else has access.

If the O-5 want people to give sightings of Dr. Spencer why would they cover his eyes? I would find a different image if you can't fully show that one.

The forewords are a bit confusing, I didn't immediately know you were talking about the d class, so some disambiguation about that would be good.

Another thing about Test 1 is Dr. Spencer seems oddly unclinical, his words themselves make grammatical sense but it definitely doesn't seem clinical. He should be stating things more factually, instead of words like "hey", "you're welcome", or "lots". It just seems like he should be less replying to the D class, and more telling him what to do in a stricter way.

The diary seems good to me, clinical tone isn't required obviously, but it does seem a bit hamfisted at the end there when he mentions the scp and how he wants to use it all in one sentence at the end.

I thought Test 2 was nice, but it felt a bit forced when you said "Always talked about the 1969 Moon landing". And again, I don't really think a doctor should be saying "hey" during procedure.

The second diary entry seemed better, because it was already established that he wanted to use the elevator, so I don't think a change needs to be present in my opinion.

I like that in the 3rd test, you specify that you're talking about the D-class this time, but I'm not sure why it didn't happen before. The Foreword of this is by far the best of the 3, it doesn't feel especially forced and gives a nice overview of the D class. The test itself seemed fine, but again, Dr. Spencer seems way too non-clinical. Also I don't think there's such a thing as Kauai Beach. Kauai is an Island in Hawaii, but I may be wrong on there being no beach.

Final diary is alright, but I'm confused how he managed to nab 2 pills of scp-500, as those are under super strict lockdown with weight sensors. I also thought the reference to 939 was forced, and there wasn't any mention of him working anywhere near those before.

Overall, the most glaring issues were it being esoteric, the test logs being non-clinical and there were a lot of things that came out of nowhere, like the 939 reference, the moon landing bit, or the sudden diary entry saying he wanted to use the elevator.

Although it might sound like I don't like it, I think this is actually a pretty solid idea, and one that could work really well. As was said in previous thread's criticism, there are other transportation scps, but I can't remember any very similar to this. I would also add a bit more to the description, like if they can interact with the other people there (if any), and if they can, what it looks like to the people in those locations when the elevator comes in (this could be determined by having someone go, finding out their favorite location, sending people to that area, then sending them again).

item.title: SCP Mermaids of the Midnight Zone: Re: SCP Mermaids of the Midnight Zone
item.content:encoded:
Was asked to take a look at this. I've got a kind of list of items I want to go over, moving from small to big, if you'll bear with me.

+ show block
– hide block

SCP-X instances are believed to operate globally.

This seems unlikely to me. How does this thing adapt to different sections of the oceans like that?

In addition, all possess an exceptionally long illicium capable of extending at least 100m, and terminating into a realistic and anatomically accurate body of a human female, connected at the base of the skull.

These human lures act as a direct extension of SCP-X, showing them to possess corresponding intellect and the ability to speak.

Honestly, I'd prefer if the process here were a little more imperfect, like the lure has the general shape of a woman but in daylight it's obviously some kind of growth, or their capacity for speak and intellect is rudimentary at best. It just kinda grounds the idea, I think.

Due to SCP-X’s anomalous abilities, all tank maintenance, feedings, tests, and interviews are to be conducted solely by biologically female staff.
…
These effects are greatly amplified in biologically male individuals.

I do not think the phrase "biologically female/male" in an SCP has ever resulted in anything good. The fixation on biology isn't particularly necessary in the context of what you're doing, anyways, and adding a compulsive effect to amplify victim's desire to have sex with the fish comes with its own host of problems.

Yes, we were attacked by a madman at knifepoint.

This whole thing is a significant amount of information pushed into a small space — why not create an addendum separate from the description to convey this in a more natural manner?

Overall it's got the general shape of an article that I'd like — it's short and it's got a little twist of expectations at the end — but I feel like the way you're communicating that twist lacks a level of nuance. Having the fish state their motivations is a bit of an anticlimax. In addition I can't really develop sympathy for the SCP since I get its motivations, but it's still manufacturing victims' desire to breed and overriding their consent. I feel like you're trying to get me to realize that these fish are just lonely but I'm not convinced.

item.title: The Abyss is Safe, Looking For Co-Authors: Re: The Safe, Dark Deep
item.content:encoded:
Overall, I'm a big fan of the way the article and story is presented. I like the way the logs record the slow degradation of the mental state of the team, and the eventual total breakdown of order. While it's nothing too original, it contains a pretty interesting narrative and SCP.

+ Some Crit
- Hide Crit

SCP-XXXX holds two main anomalous properties.

This sentence and the use of "Firstly" and "Secondly" is a bit extraneous. I don't really see a need to state that their are two main anomalous properties when we are about to read them.

Hume readings in the area are incredibly low, indicating some force inside the cavern is altering reality. The side effects of this property make it so that conventional methods of terminating living organisms do not work (for reference please see Dr. Anna Lang’s research and SCP-3001).

SCP-3001 is my personal favorite, so I'm glad to see it being referenced here. However, one of the major effects of low hume levels as presented in that article is that they cause the disintegration of physical matter over time. This isn't too much of a problem, since the cave's regenerative factors likely make up for this, but it might needed to be directly stated in the article if that's the case.

There are a pretty large amount of grammatical errors in the description and some in the logs. I just suggest giving these another once-over for errors.

Also, having read the Idea thread, I personally prefer "The Abyss is Safe" for the title. It sounds a bit more original and eye catching to me.

item.title: “Green Crabs” they’re always green: Re: “Green Crabs” they’re always green
item.content:encoded:
Collapsed for ease of scrolling.

+ show block
– hide block

Crabs: Overall I was aiming to connect the crabs with the cancer constellation through the dates of the journal entries being the day that the constellation is represented to the end date that it is represented, I believe I can make this more evident however.

Then how would the constellation’s prevalence relate to the art and the artist’s rage? That seems like another tenuous connection.

Diary Pages: I see what you mean, overall I was aiming to do a slow progression into hatred of the art, but it appears it wasn’t visible, I assume having a distinct part where it appears to be teetering into hatred would make it easier? Overall I presume a reworking would help?

If anything, I’d almost recommend leaning into his self-assurance that this will be his masterpiece. I think you’d be able to make it clear that he dislikes it through over-enthusiastic optimism, if that makes sense.

I have to say, I’m a little confused when it comes to the bit about the paint not sticking to the painting. Is that a motif I’m not getting, or something about the paint that I missed?

Also I aimed to leave the artist’s death to user interpretation either scheele’s green as you mentioned or the first activation of SCP-XXXX-1. The death’s contents can change depending on what the final few diary entries indicate I presume.

I can appreciate the meaningful ambiguity, but at the moment, the ending entry feels a tad anti-climactic. I think that a more carefully handled progression of self-hatred might help with that.

item.title: Try again? Fugitive vs the Yakuza: Re: Try again? Fugitive vs the Yakuza
item.content:encoded:
Placeholder! Got summoned via PM to take a look-see. Will crit in a bit.

Alright, here’s my take.

+ show block
– hide block

First of all, I’d suggest seeking out a critiquer with experience in line-by-line and structural critique. There were definitely some typos here and there, and the lack of line breaks in some places made it difficult to parse through.

It’s also difficult for me to judge this piece on its own, frankly. It’s very obviously part of a series, considering how ‘Honey’ would be quite a wasted element otherwise. Whether or not this story stands on its own two feet, however, depends on the action prose. Whether that works, in turn, depends on its flow. At the moment, the majority of your fight scenes are crammed into single paragraphs. I’d recommend respacing those a bit to let your scenes breathe.

Besides that, I’m afraid I don’t have much experience when it comes to the first element in a series. I know it can be a tricky thing to do, especially considering the need to establish stakes and characters. I’d recommend also reaching out to a critter with experience in series or serial tales.


If you respond to this comment and would like me to see it, please send me a Wikidot PM, as I will not be notified otherwise.

item.title: SCP-something: Man unable to communicate properly: Re: SCP-something: Man unable to communicate properly
item.content:encoded:
Of the new stuff you've added, I have to say that the end of the new interview might be the most compelling part. At its core, the emotionally compelling elements here are centered around SCPxx's struggle to communicate what it perceives as a terrifying threat. The actual threat may or may not exist, but the truly evocative lines in this come from SCPxx's frustration and desperation. I'd recommend leaning into that.

I'd also like to echo my previous recommendation to reconsider some of your redactions. As discussed in MalyceGraves' exceptional guide on the subject, the style you're utilizing here isn't the best way to communicate your plot.

item.title: Draft "Disconnected Restroom": Re: Draft "Disconnected Restroom"
item.content:encoded:
Okay, here goes:

+ show block
– hide block

Immediately from the containment, the information is rather jumbled. Try to structure the containment from establishing the most immediately pertinent visualization aspects first (in this case, the fact that the anomaly is in a provisional site) and then moving from subject to subject for each aspect of requirements (staffing, maintenance, access, etc.). Also, try to trim down the length of the sentences that are simple "don't do this" commands. For example:

It is only to be entered by Level 2 cleared staff and only for research or cleaning purposes.

No water originating from SCP-XXXX is to be used for cleaning and no liquids from outside of SCP-XXX are to be inserted into the facilities.

At no time should SCP-XXXX be used as sanitary facility.

You could just make a quick bullet list with parallel structure so the directions aren't as roundabout. For example:

Personnel accessing SCP-XXXX may not:

  • Enter the anomaly if not performing research or cleaning.
  • Use water produced by SCP-XXXX for cleaning.
  • Insert liquids from outside SCP-XXXX into the facility.
  • Use SCP-XXXX as a sanitary facility.

Remember that clinical tone does not mean using a lot of words to describe something simple. In that same vein, you don't need to use phrases like "at no time" and "at all times" since it's assumed that unless otherwise stated, containment procedures are always in place.

There are also a lot of small errors, such as:

  • Typically authorization levels have hyphens. So Level-2 and not Level 2.
  • Vague instructions. "Cleaning staff are to flush if they hear noises coming from SCP-XXXX" > what exactly are they flushing? What sort of noises?
  • and must make record of doing so. > there should be a standardized log system rather than just "record it somewhere". Ideally, there would be some sort of cleaning report that could be referenced for this sort of thing. "Make record" could be anything from a cell phone call to a post-it note to a formal write-up.
  • I'm not certain if "port-a-potty" would be considered clinical phrasing. "Portable toilet" or "alternative restroom facilities" would be taken more seriously.
  • SCP-XXXX is to be locked at all times unless Level 2 staff requires to enter the SCP. > this should be placed earlier in the instructions. Also, Level-2 staff is a very wide body of individuals; it would make more sense to just note "personnel assigned to SCP-XXXX" or the like. Also, don't refer to an anomaly as "the SCP" (SCP refers to the containment procedures or the Foundation motto). In-universe, the non-slang way to reference this anomaly would just be "SCP-XXXX" or "the restrooms".
  • and so on.

The description is similarly full of small errors in clinical tone and Foundation presentation; the most notable issue is that the anomalous effects are not made immediately clear. There's no need to have the background investigation noted before the effects of drinking the tap water. This is another case where a bullet-point list could be of use, to introduce all of the small anomalous effects together so the reader isn't left wondering why the Foundation bothered containing the location.

The Audio Transcript portion just feels a little sloppily written because the dialogue feels wooden (Frank in particular sounds more like a robot trying to imitate human speech than an actual human talking in the moment) and there are again small errors ("lets" is missing an apostrophe). As a reader, I'm unsure of what the log is meant to convey besides typical "something unknown but bad happened because the place is spooky and something happened to the robot" tension. It feels a little forced and as a result I feel skeptical more than scared.

The Incident Report just feels almost tacked on as an afterthought. I'm not sure why "Michael" needed to be italicized, and the suddenness of the anomaly hurting someone and behaving oddly comes kind of out of nowhere. It would have been better pacing if that sort of effect had been introduced or at least more clearly hinted at in the description. And then at the end of the incident report I as a reader am still unsure about what's going on and why I should care about the anomaly. It messes with people's digestive systems apparently… for what reason? If you don't intend to have an in-universe reason for the manifestation, there needs to at least be a more meaningful takeaway at the end of the article (could have been something like "is the Foundation justified in starving the thing?" or "should the Foundation try to introduce appetite suppressants?") beyond just "okay it can actually do scary things, update the containment".

Overall I feel like the article needs a fair bit of general restructuring so the basic anomaly information and plot flow better. The storyline in particular needs to move more fluidly from the description to the addenda; right now each part feels almost like separate portions of the story with the in-between material removed. As such, it feels jumpy and sudden and disconnected, rather than a followable investigative process of understanding the anomaly.

item.title: SCP Mermaids of the Midnight Zone: Re: SCP Mermaids of the Midnight Zone
item.content:encoded:
Have been summoned by PM, so here I come. Pighead In, here's a short review of your draft.

So, this is pretty good when it comes to the writing, but I have two issues with it. The first, the main one, is the fact that for me, the end is really abrupt. The entire thing is pretty short and when I came to the end of the interview, I was like "That's all?". I felt like there were more things that you could tell, about why SCP XXX-1 wants to find love, about the feelings of isolation it could have (and who were really briefly touched upon on the very last sentence).

And the second thing is that at this moment, for me, this draft is "Mermaid, but SCP". Like, I feel like I just see a mermaid who is adapted into an SCP. And not that I'm against mythological creatures being turned into SCPs, the history of the site had proved that it could work really efficiently. But with the really short draft, that creates a situation when it's not really interesting to see this, it's like "So, here's this mythological creature and its abilities and nothing else".

What I can suggest to you is to dig deeper into how the mermaids live as a society, what are their collective purpose in life and what is the backstory of SCP-XXXX-1, what are the events who led it to wanting a mate, a person to love, what led it to wanting not just having intercourse, but having a person for spending the rest of its life with. With that, you have the potential to tell a pretty good story about how isolation and being tired of just doing what you have to do can led you to wanting something new in life and experiencing, for the first time, human feelings.

So, think about all that, for the rest, your writing has potential. It's all for me, Pighead Out.
